stations.title: Station 1: Introduction to AI & K-NN Classifier 🧱
stations.desc: Discover the magical differences between AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning, and write your first K-NN distance algorithm!
stations.story:
🎯 Session Agenda:

  • Introduction to AI vs. Machine Learning vs. Deep Learning
  • Examples of AI (Virtual Assistants, Self-Driving Cars, Robotics)
  • What is an Algorithm?
  • The K-NN (K-Nearest Neighbor) Supervised Learning algorithm
  • How K-NN works step-by-step

📘 AI vs. Machine Learning vs. Deep Learning

  • Artificial Intelligence (AI): The ability of a machine to imitate intelligent human behavior (like Siri, self-driving cars, or robot chess players).
  • Machine Learning (ML): A special application of AI that allows a system to automatically learn and improve from experience without being explicitly programmed (like product recommendations and image classification).
  • Deep Learning (DL): An advanced type of machine learning that uses complex neural networks with many layers to train models on big datasets.

📐 What is an Algorithm?

An algorithm is a step-by-step procedure used to solve a problem or perform a computation, acting like a highly detailed recipe for the computer to follow.

🎯 The K-NN (K-Nearest Neighbor) Algorithm

K-NN is one of the simplest supervised learning algorithms. It classifies a new, unknown data point based on the majority vote of its closest coordinate neighbors in a graphic space!

📐 Euclidean Distance Formula

To find the closest neighbors, K-NN uses Euclidean Distance, which represents the shortest straight line between two coordinate points:
distance = sqrt((x2 - x1)**2 + (y2 - y1)**2)
stations.simple: AI is like a super-smart robot, Machine Learning is how it learns by practicing, and Deep Learning is a brain-like neural network! The K-NN algorithm is like deciding where to sit at school: if most programming kids sit at a desk next to you, you classify yourself as a programmer too!

stations.title: Station 2: Computer Vision & Face Detection with OpenCV 📷
stations.desc: Discover how the computer sees the world, import the legendary OpenCV library, and locate hero faces!
stations.story:
🎯 Session Agenda:

  • Human vs. Computer Vision systems
  • Required Libraries (NumPy and OpenCV)
  • Installing packages using the terminal
  • What is OpenCV?
  • The Haar Cascade face detection algorithm

👁️ Human Vision vs. Computer Vision

  • Human Vision System: A biological system composed of eyes, optic nerves, and brain cells that perceive and interpret visual data instantly in real-time.
  • Computer Vision System: An artificial AI system designed to emulate human vision. It uses digital cameras, image pixel grids, and algorithms to capture and extract information from visual streams.

📥 Required Packages

To build vision systems, we import two essential libraries:
  • Numpy: For fast mathematical grid and matrix array calculations.
  • OpenCV (opencv-python): A powerful open-source library packed with tools to solve computer vision problems. Install it using the terminal command: pip install opencv-python

🕵️‍♂️ Haar Cascade Face Detection

OpenCV uses the Haar Cascade Algorithm to identify faces. It detects 'Haar-like features' (areas of dark and light region intensities) and calculates the sum differences to quickly isolate facial shapes (like eyes, nose bridge, and cheeks).
stations.simple: The human eyes send pictures to the brain, and the camera sends pixel coordinate numbers to OpenCV! The Haar Cascade is like Snapchat filters; it searches for light and shadow patterns on your face to draw a rectangular box around it immediately!

PyWhatKit is an easy-to-use Python library with various helpful automation features. It allows us to automate repetitive tasks like sending WhatsApp messages or opening videos on YouTube using simple Python commands! Install it using the command: pip install pywhatkit.

💬 ChatGPT & Large Language Models (LLM)

ChatGPT is a natural language processing tool driven by AI technology developed by OpenAI. It is built on top of GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 families of Large Language Models (LLM) neural networks.

💡 What does GPT stand for?

Generative Pre-trained Transformer: A type of neural network trained on billions of text books to answer questions, summarize paragraphs, and even write coding scripts!

⚖️ Rule-Based Bots vs. Generative AI

  • Rule-Based Bots: Traditional chatbots that follow strict, pre-programmed rules ('if this, then do that'). They cannot understand context or unexpected replies.
  • Generative AI: Smart models that continuously learn, understanding flexible human conversations and generating new custom responses!

stations.title: Station 5: Deep Learning & CNN Architecture 🕸️
stations.desc: Dive deep into neural network layers, weight sharing, and build a convolutional network coordinate architecture!
stations.story:
🎯 Session Agenda:

  • Deep Learning & how it simulates the human brain
  • Human Brain neurons vs. Computer
  • Image Representation (Pixels stored in Coordinate arrays)
  • Supervised vs. Unsupervised Learning
  • What is a CNN (Convolutional Neural Network)?
  • CNN Layers: Convolutional, Pooling, Flattening, Dense

🧠 Human Brain vs. Computer

Our brains consist of 100 billion nerve cells (neurons) that detect, receive, and transmit visual features. In Deep Learning, we attempt to simulate this behavior using artificial networks!

🕸️ What is a CNN?

A Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) is a deep learning algorithm specially designed for working with images and videos. Unlike Fully Connected (FC) networks, CNN layers share filter weights (Weight Sharing) to dramatically reduce calculation parameters and preserve local pixel patterns!

🛠️ The Four Essential CNN Layers:

  1. Convolutional Layer: Slides filters across the pixel grid to find edges and extract features.
  2. Pooling Layer: Downsizes the feature maps to save computing memory while keeping the most important information.
  3. Flattening Layer: Converts a multi-dimensional 2D image matrix into a single 1D linear array.
  4. Dense (Full Connection) Layer: Links every neuron to classify the image category.
stations.simple: Your brain classifies a drawing by looking at lines and corners first. A CNN does the exact same thing! It takes an image, extracts features using 'filters' in the Convolution layer, downsizes it in the Pooling layer, flattens it, and then guesses what's in the picture!

stations.desc: Train a model on Google Teachable Machine, export a lightweight TFLite file, and normalize visual pixels!
stations.story:

🎯 Google Teachable Machine

Teachable Machine is a scond-to-none website from Google that lets you train classification models using your camera, voice, or pictures! You upload images into class labels, click Train, and export the trained classifier.

📦 TFLite (TensorFlow Lite)

We export models as lightweight .tflite files, optimized to run super-fast on mobile phones and small computers.

🖼️ Image Pre-processing & Pixel Normalization

Computers read images as 2D grids of pixel intensity numbers (0 to 255). To help neural networks calculate faster and prevent errors, we perform **Normalization** by dividing the pixel values by 255.0. This scales all coordinates beautifully between 0.0 and 1.0! We also add a batch dimension (shape [1, 224, 224, 3]) using np.expand_dims because models expect inputs in batches.
stations.simple: Teachable Machine lets you teach a computer using your webcam or photos! Normalizing is like shrinking giant giant numbers between 0 and 255 into tiny friendly numbers between 0.0 and 1.0, so the AI model's brain doesn't get a headache calculating them!

stations.desc: Master the 5 critical stages of Machine Learning, avoid the 'Garbage In, Garbage Out' trap, and organize datasets!
stations.story:
🎯 Session Agenda:

  • Data Collection: finding online, pre-made, or drawing your own datasets

  • Drawing datasets (Hearts, Stars, Flowers) using ML for Kids

🔄 The 5 Steps of Machine Learning Projects

Every professional artificial intelligence project follows these five steps:
  1. Problem Definition: Decide exactly what problem you want your AI model to solve.
  2. Data Collection: Gather high-quality training examples (images, voice recordings, or coordinate lists).
  3. Data Preparation: Clean and format the data (normalizing, cropping, and naming labels).
  4. Model Training: Feed the dataset into an algorithm so it learns the features.
  5. Evaluation: Test the trained model's accuracy on brand-new, unseen data.

🗑️ The 'Garbage In, Garbage Out' Rule

This is the number-one golden rule of Data Science! If your training data is of low quality, badly cropped, or incorrectly labeled, your trained AI model will make terrible, garbage predictions. Quality data equals quality AI!

🎨 Creating Custom Datasets

In this project, we draw 15 different coordinate drawings of Hearts, Stars, and Flowers inside ML for Kids, teaching the computer the distinct vectors and features of each shape.
stations.simple: Before training a dog, you must show it treats! Machine Learning is the same: first we must collect clean drawings. The 'Garbage In, Garbage Out' rule means that if you teach a robot using bad, messy drawings, the robot will make silly mistakes and fail its tests!

📦 Requirements File (requirements.txt)

A requirements.txt file is a standard text file that lists all external library dependencies required by a Python project. It allows developers to configure their workspace and install all modules at once with one command:
pip install -r requirements.txt

🔗 What is an API?

An API (Application Programming Interface) is a digital software bridge that allows your Python code to talk to an online server. We send the user's test drawing to the ML for Kids online model server using a secure **API Key**, and the server sends back the classification prediction instantly!

🔄 Iterating Predictions

We write Python loops to iterate through a list of new drawings, query the model API, extract the predicted label, and print the model's confidence level percentage (how sure the AI is!).
stations.simple: An API is like a waiter in a restaurant: you ask for a shape prediction (the order), the API takes it to the trained AI model (the kitchen), and brings you back the result (the food)! Secure API keys act like your private password so only your code can talk to the model!

stations.desc: Differentiate face detection from object detection, load deep weights in DNN, and clean data text!
stations.story:

  • What is Object Detection? (Bounding Boxes and category Labels)

📦 Face Detection vs. Object Detection

  • Face Detection: Looks exclusively for human face shapes.
  • Object Detection: A powerful computer vision technique that identifies, labels, and locates hundreds of different object categories (like cars, cups, dogs, and pedestrians) in images or live camera streams, framing them in Bounding Boxes.

📡 OpenCV DNN Module

The **DNN (Deep Neural Network)** module in OpenCV is highly optimized to run pre-trained neural networks. We use the class cv2.dnn_DetectionModel to easily load binary weights (containing the model's intelligence) and network configurations (describing the layer layouts).

⚙️ String Cleanups during Label Loading

When loading object class labels from text files, we write Python string cleaners:
  • strip(): Removes leading/trailing spaces and newline symbols (\n).
  • split(): Breaks a coordinate string into individual words or elements based on a separator.
stations.simple: Face detection only looks for eyes and noses. Object detection looks for everything! It places a rectangle (Bounding Box) around a chair, a phone, or a cup and labels it. DNN is like a super-fast engine in OpenCV that runs massive, pre-trained neural networks!

⚡ What is Roboflow?

Roboflow is a scond-to-none web portal designed to organize custom datasets! Even with a small number of custom pictures, you can annotate, train, and deploy professional object detection models easily.

✏️ Image Annotation (Labeling)

Annotation is the process of drawing box coordinates around your specific custom items (like a customized toy robot or keyholder) and labeling them with their class names. This teaches the custom neural network exactly what to search for!

⚖️ Confidence Thresholds

When testing models, the AI outputs a confidence score (from 0% to 100%) indicating how sure it is about each Bounding Box prediction. We set a **Confidence Threshold** (e.g., 50%) to ignore weak, incorrect guesses and show only true, high-confidence detections!
stations.simple: Roboflow is like an online art studio where you upload pictures and draw rectangles around toys, labeling them so the computer learns their shapes. The confidence threshold is like a filter: if a robot says 'I am only 20% sure this is a car,' we filter it out so we only see smart, high-percentage answers!

✋ MediaPipe & cvzone Skeletons

  • MediaPipe: A fantastic Google framework designed to perform high-speed body tracking, joint skeletons, and face meshes.
  • cvzone: A brilliant package that wraps OpenCV and MediaPipe in extremely simple, developer-friendly Python statements. Install them using: pip install cvzone mediapipe

🎥 Setting Video Properties

When starting the camera, we adjust the frame sizes using property IDs:
  • Property ID 3: Changes the webcam frame Width.
  • Property ID 4: Changes the webcam frame Height.

📍 Skeletons & Bounding Landmarks

MediaPipe runs a high-speed **Palm Detection** first to crop the hand area. Then it maps **21 distinct hand landmarks** representing skeletal coordinates, allowing us to count raised fingers instantly using the fingersUp() method!
stations.simple: MediaPipe is like a digital skeletal glove that snaps coordinate trackers to your wrist and finger joints! It detects 21 key points on your hand. The fingersUp() function returns a list like [0, 1, 1, 0, 0] to show that only your Index and Middle fingers are raised!

stations.story:

  • Constructing countdown timers using cv2.putText()
  • Numeric choice mapping (Rock = 1, Paper = 2, Scissors = 3)

  • Maintaining scoreboard score list trackers

🎮 The Interactive Game Loop

In this final stop, we merge everything into a unified game! We use state variables like startGame to trigger rounds and stateResult to track if the computer has decided a winner.

⏳ Countdown overlays

We draw a countdown timer (3, 2, 1) directly on the screen using cv2.putText(), which overlays custom BGR colored text strings at precise coordinates.

⚖️ Victory Comparison Logic

To calculate who wins each round, we map choices numerically (Rock = 1, Paper = 2, Scissors = 3). We apply logical conditions:
  • Player Victory conditions:
    1. Player has Rock (1) and AI has Scissors (3)
    2. Player has Paper (2) and AI has Rock (1)
    3. Player has Scissors (3) and AI has Paper (2)
  • If choices are equal, it's a tie round! Otherwise, the AI wins the round!
